note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — SHORT RAMES IN A SILVERY HEAD
tiles.details: Start with Matt Lavin's genuine silvery panicle (panel 0), then see Austin flowering habitat (panel 7). Trace the MANY SHORT crowded hairy flowering branches along a central axis, not just their white hairs. Compare introduced KR (panel 4): several longer finger-like terminal racemes. A detached fuzzy head alone is insufficient.
tiles.short: Many short crowded hairy flowering branches form a narrow cottony plume
tiles.status: AUTHENTIC LICENSED SEEDHEAD PHOTOGRAPHED; whole crown-to-head sequence missing

tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED CROWN AND RHIZOME CAUTION
tiles.details: Finally, physical CC0 Denver Botanic Gardens and Smithsonian source-vouchered silver herbarium photographs show actual EXPOSED ROOTS attached to BASAL SHOOT CROWNS, unlike the earlier Arizona standing clump with its roots hidden. The complete real specimens are from Colorado and New Mexico respectively; do NOT claim verified Hays County live rhizomes or stolons from preserved-root pictures. Trace upper flowering shoots down through the shared shoot base into attached roots. Native silver is typically bunch-forming; short rhizome reports vary among regional floras.
tiles.short: Perennial bunchgrass; some sources document short rhizomes
tiles.status: ROOTED PHOTO ROLE NOW COVERED: two CC0 cataloged true plant-root sheets plus original Arizona flowering clump; local living rhizome form still unresolved

tiles.heading: 03 · LOOK AT THE TRUE CULM NODES AND LIGULE
tiles.details: See new actual Texas panels 17, 18, 19 in order: opened INNER leaf collar with pale unmeasured transverse rim; separate dark purple-brown TRUE culm node; OUTER leaf-sheath junction. Compare prior photographed true nodes (11–12) and Denton blade–sheath junction (9). Do not teach a measured ligule, constant node color or hairlessness where no calibrated scale is pictured.
tiles.short: Usually pale, smooth-to-short-haired nodes; a genuine ~2 mm membrane
tiles.status: REAL SPECIES-VERIFIED TEXAS OPENED COLLAR AND CULM NODES — millimeter scale still missing

tiles.heading: 04 · SEE THE SPIKELET PAIR, NOT JUST FLUFF
tiles.details: Liz Makings' Arizona macro (panel 5) resolves an elongated spikelet, bent/twisted awn and long pale hairs. NEW independently licensed, research-grade 2026 Deer Park Texas close-up (panel 9) also shows several oblong golden spikelet bodies with long silk on a genuine flowering segment. Two arrows identify visible bodies and hair ONLY; neither picture proves exact sessile fertile/pedicelled sterile attachments or upper fertile lemma awn insertion. Bob Harms BOLAT-s and BOLAT-9 remain original copyrighted external scientific references; don't invent mm-scale organ labels.
tiles.short: Sessile fertile unit alongside a smaller pedicelled sterile unit
tiles.status: PARTIAL 0.5/1 — Arizona spikelet and Texas flowering segment both visibly photographed; connected paired organs and 1mm scale still missing

tiles.heading: 05 · DISTINGUISH THE BENT AWN FROM SILKY HAIRS
tiles.details: See the actual BENT AWN on Liz Makings' physically archived Arizona panel 5 and compare to the pale flexible surrounding hairs. Its point of origin from the upper fertile lemma of a sessile spikelet is a published botanical claim, not anatomically traced to a visible insertion in the present 720×540 image. Bob Harms' copyrighted BOLAT-9 macro (panel 3) supplies additional external context. We need a dissected linked specimen with mm scale before labeling any particular lemma or glume.
tiles.short: The upper fertile lemma bears one longer bent/twisted awn
tiles.status: AWN AND SILK visibly documented with arrows; measured fertile-lemma insertion NOT photographed

tiles.heading: 06 · LOOK-ALIKES AND PUBLICATION GATE
tiles.details: Seven documented noncommercial site-permitted silver bluestem photographs now live in the GitHub species images directory: two New Mexico Matt Lavin CC BY-SA, one Arizona Liz Makings spikelet, one Arizona Max Licher connected flowering clump, one Austin smallcurio CC BY, and NEW 2026 Texas CC BY-NC leaf–sheath junction from Denton and hairy flowering group from Deer Park. Three historical images remain rights/ID held and excluded. Two copyright-retained Bob Harms originals remain external educational references, and three Dan Tenaglia Kansas microscopic comparison sources LINK ONLY. Silver's numerous short silky rames contrast with introduced KR's relatively fewer, longer terminal fingers; verify multiple characters before any removal. NEW TWO TEX Herbarium real rooted flowering plants with attached fibrous roots and clear CC BY 4.0 image permissions add the previously missing basal/root anatomy; these are pressed specimens (Guadalupe/Gaines County), not field-grown comparison photographs. No claim of absent rhizomes or photographed free ligule.
tiles.short: Silver vs cane vs KR: node hairs, rame lengths, and a measured pair
tiles.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — 9 public-usable physically archived species photos; real Texas node photographed, measured true ligule, exposed roots and linked mm spikelet pair outstanding

steps.title: 1 · Start with a full silvery flowering head
steps.look_for: Notice many crowded SHORT silky flowering branches along a longer, narrow central flowering axis in this real New Mexico plant.
steps.why_it_matters: Head architecture is more dependable than silver-white color; do not count every silky hair as a separate branch.

steps.title: 2 · Find the connected bunch
steps.look_for: Follow the upright flowering culms down to the actual connected BASAL SHOOT CLUMP in this Arizona photo. The roots are underground and are NOT photographed.
steps.why_it_matters: This confirms the grass is a clump-forming perennial; it does not demonstrate that rhizomes are absent. Texas botanical sources disagree on short rhizome presence.

steps.title: 3 · See actual roots attached to the crown
steps.look_for: The real Denver Botanic Gardens herbarium specimen shows a joined basal crown with ACTUAL fibrous roots still physically attached; arrowheads mark only visible plant parts. This specimen was collected in Colorado, not Hays County.
steps.why_it_matters: Distinguishes a photographed perennial base from an aboveground bunch whose roots are hidden. This does not establish whether a local live Texas stand has short rhizomes.

steps.title: 4 · Open the INNER collar to locate the ligule
steps.look_for: Linda Jo Conn's species-identified Milam County, Texas photograph shows the sheath opened to expose a short pale transverse inner lip. No physical 1-mm ruler is present.
steps.why_it_matters: This is where to inspect the real membranous ligule. Do not confuse the leaf sheath with the membrane or claim a measured 1–3 mm length.

steps.title: 5 · Find a true node on the CULM
steps.look_for: In a second photograph of the same Texas specimen, find the actual transverse purple-brown stem band along the pale upright stem. The adjacent green leaf blade is not a node.
steps.why_it_matters: A culm node and the leaf collar are different structures; node color and hairiness vary, and this photograph has no 1-mm ruler.

steps.title: 6 · Check the photographed spikelet and its bent awn
steps.look_for: See the tan elongated spikelet body, fine surrounding pale hairs and an extended DARK bent awn in Liz Makings' original microscope photograph.
steps.why_it_matters: Awns are different structures from hairs. The true attached fertile sessile/pedicelled partner pair and upper lemma awn insertion are not visible at organ-level certainty in this photo.

steps.title: 7 · Separate silver from invasive King Ranch
steps.look_for: This is real TEXAS KR bluestem, not silver: trace several much LONGER terminal fingers to their attachment points, then return to photo 1 and its numerous short silvery branches.
steps.why_it_matters: Confusing native silver with introduced KR can lead to unnecessary removal; also check a real cane bluestem true culm node for its long shaggy beard.

panels.label: INTRODUCED LOOK-ALIKE — King Ranch bluestem (Texas flowering head)
panels.caption: King Ranch bluestem may also appear silky, but its racemes are often longer than the central panicle axis and spread as a smaller subdigitate cluster. Compare silver bluestem's densely aggregated many short racemes. Check actual leaf-base papilla-based hairs and paired spikelets before deciding; head silhouette alone is not sufficient.

intro: Walk from the narrow cottony flowering head and a living clump through an actual rooted voucher, then see Texas photographs of the OPENED INNER blade–sheath collar and the actual CULM NODE. Finish with the awned spikelet and the invasive King Ranch bluestem comparison. Real photographs; the Texas membrane and node lack millimeter calibration, and an intact measured spikelet pair is still missing.
memory_rule: SILVER = numerous SHORT fluffy racemes together in a narrow plume; KR = relatively FEWER LONG finger-like terminal racemes. Confirm with true node/ligule and spikelet evidence before native-grass removal decisions.
safety_note: Do not remove native candidates based on color or one node. The new source-verified Texas collar and node photographs are real and correctly annotated, but not calibrated. An actual 1-mm-measured ligule and intact attached sessile/pedicelled spikelet pair remain genuine research-photo gaps. Nonlocal rooted herbarium specimens do not prove local live rhizomes.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Silver bluestem: narrow contracted oblong densely silvery head with many short rames and typically pale, glabrous nodes. Cane bluestem: wider fanlike many-branched panicle and a thick hair beard at true nodes. KR bluestem: several longer, slender fingerlike racemes clustered at the tip; node hairiness varies and is not proof. Bushy bluestem: broad brushy crown built of paired spathe-subtended rames; inspect inflorescence architecture rather than white color alone.

morphology.habit: Warm-season perennial, usually tufted/bunch-forming with sometimes semi-prostrate lower culms. ROOT BASE SOURCE CONFLICT: Texas A&M's legacy subsp. torreyana account describes no rhizomes; the UT Williamson County specimen treatment explicitly describes short horizontal rhizomes (to ~4 mm diameter) and basal adventitious roots. Do not certify or reject silver bluestem from rhizome presence/absence alone; document the actual connected crown.
morphology.leaves: Many leaves are basal; blades are flat, rough on the upper surface and margins.
morphology.inflorescence: Contracted narrow panicle containing many short rames; dense pale hairs make the flowering/fruiting head look silver-white and cottony.
morphology.spikelets: Paired spikelets occur on the rames; sessile spikelets are awned, with long surrounding hairs contributing to the silver appearance.

eco_habitat: Dry prairies, limestone and rocky sites, roadsides, and open grasslands in Central, South, and West Texas.
